title: Conditions, loops & characters (book exercises)
overview: Short exercises from the textbook chapter on decisions and repetition. They cover `if / else`, `for`, `while` and `do-while` loops, and the idea that a `char` is really a small number (its ASCII code). Together these let a program choose what to do and repeat work.

concepts.explain: Runs one block when a condition is true and the other block when it is false.
Checks conditions from top to bottom and runs only the first block whose condition is true.
`a<=b && a<=c` is true only when both parts are true. This is how you test 'a is the smallest of three'.
`'a'` is stored as 97 and `'A'` as 65. Lowercase and uppercase letters are exactly 32 apart, so `ch - 32` turns `'g'` into `'G'`.
`ch >= '0' && ch <= '9'` checks whether a character is a digit. Use `>=` and `<=` so both ends of the range count.
`for` suits a known number of repeats. `while` checks its condition before each round. `do-while` checks after each round, so its body always runs at least once.

files.title: Even or odd
files.what: Reads a number and says whether it is even or odd, using the remainder after dividing by 2.
steps: `n % 2` is the remainder after dividing by 2: 0 for even numbers, 1 for odd numbers.
If the remainder is 0, print `Even number`. Otherwise print `Odd number`.

check.q: What is `-7 % 2` in C, and does this program still work for negative odd numbers?
check.a: It is -1. The program only checks `== 0`, so -7 is still correctly called odd.

files.title: Minimum and maximum of three numbers
files.what: Reads three numbers and prints the smallest one, then the largest one, using if / else-if ladders with `&&`.
steps: If `a` is less than or equal to both others, it is the minimum. Otherwise test `b` the same way. If neither passes, `c` must be the minimum.
Repeat the same idea with `>=` to find the maximum.
Using `<=` (not `<`) means ties are still handled: with `5 5 9`, `a` counts as the minimum.
files.output_note: First line `3` (the minimum), second line `8` (the maximum).

check.q: Why does the last branch simply print `c` without checking anything?
check.a: If neither `a` nor `b` is the smallest, the only one left is `c`.

files.title: Swap a letter's case
files.what: Reads one letter and prints it in the opposite case by adding or subtracting 32 from its ASCII code.
steps: If `a` is between `'a'` and `'z'`, it is lowercase, so print `a - 32` (for example, 'g' = 103 becomes 71 = 'G').
Otherwise the program assumes it is uppercase and prints `a + 32`.
files.watch_out: The `else` branch adds 32 to anything that is not lowercase. A digit or symbol turns into some other character. A safer version checks `a >= 'A' && a <= 'Z'` before adding.

check.q: What is the ASCII gap between 'a' and 'A', and why is it the same for every letter?
check.a: 32. Both alphabets are laid out in the same order, so every lowercase letter is exactly 32 above its uppercase letter.

files.title: Digit, small or capital?
files.what: Classifies a character as a digit, or as a letter and then as small or capital. It uses an if / else with another if / else inside it (a nested if).
steps: If `x` is between `'0'` and `'9'`, print `IS DIGIT`.
Otherwise print `ALPHA`, then use an inner if to decide between `IS SMALL` and `IS CAPITAL`.
files.output_note: For `b` you get two lines: `ALPHA`, then `IS SMALL`.
files.watch_out: The inner test is `x > 'a' && x < 'z'`, so `a` and `z` are reported as capital letters. Fix: use `x >= 'a' && x <= 'z'`. Module 5's version gets this right.

check.q: Which two lowercase letters does this program misclassify, and why?
check.a: `a` and `z`. The strict `>` and `<` leave out both ends of the range, so they are reported as `IS CAPITAL`.

files.title: Counting with for loops
files.what: Two `for` loops: the first prints 1 to 10, then the second prints 1 to 30, one number per line.
steps: `for (i=1; i<=10; i++)` has three parts: start at 1, keep going while `i<=10`, and add 1 after each round.
Each round prints `i` followed by a newline.
The second loop reuses the same variable `i` and resets it to 1 before counting to 30.
files.output_note: You will see 1 to 10, then the count starts again at 1 and goes to 30 (40 lines in total).

check.q: How many times does `for (i=1; i<=30; i++)` run its body?

files.title: while vs do-while
files.what: Counts `i` up from 1 to 5 with a `while` loop, then counts `j` down from 10 to 1 with a `do-while` loop.
steps: `while (i <= 5)` checks the condition first, prints `i`, then does `i += 1`.
`do { ... } while (j > 0);` prints `j` and does `j -= 1` first, then checks whether to repeat.
files.output_note: The output shows `i = 1` to `i = 5`, then `j = 10` down to `j = 1`.

check.q: If `j` started at 0, how many lines would the do-while print?
check.a: One line (`j = 0`), because the body runs before the condition is checked.

recap: `%` gives the remainder; `n % 2 == 0` means `n` is even.
In an else-if ladder, only the first true branch runs.
Use `>=` and `<=` for ranges so both ends are included.
A do-while body always runs at least once; a while body might not run at all.

check_yourself.q: Write a condition that is true only when `ch` is an uppercase letter.
What is the difference between a `while` loop and a `do-while` loop?
check_yourself.a: A `while` loop checks its condition before each round, so it can run zero times. A `do-while` loop checks after each round, so it runs at least once.

check_yourself.q: With `a=4, b=4, c=9`, which branch of min_max.c prints the minimum?
check_yourself.a: The first one. `a<=b` and `a<=c` are both true, so it prints 4.
